title: Roller Skating: Fun and Cool
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a plug for Cooperative for Education (co-ED) fundraiser, then trace roller skating's history from 1700s English stage skates and John Joseph Merlin's 1760 skates, through James Leonard Plimpton's 1863 quad "rocking skates," Victorian rinks, the 1950s rink boom, Black American integration and Soul Nights, Bill Butler and disco-era roller disco, the polyurethane wheel, and 1970s roller disco films and TV. They cover skating styles (rhythm, jam, artistic, freestyle, Detroit sliding, Atlanta, Cleveland), inline skates and Amish teens, skate anatomy (boots, plates, trucks, toe stops, jam plugs, light-up wheels), the pandemic-era revival spurred by On Koto, a trivia note that N.W.A first performed at skate Land in Compton, and a listener mail correction about John Green (not Tom Green) and Paper Towns.
topics: listener mail John Green Paper Towns

segments.title: Intro and co-ED fundraiser plug
segments.summary: Opening banter and a plug for the Cooperative for Education fundraiser aimed at reaching one million dollars from Stuff You Should Know Army donations.

segments.title: Hosts' personal roller rink memories
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh recall being teens at roller rinks, with supervision rules, youth group outings, and awkward attempts at skating and kissing.

segments.title: Early roller skates and Merlin's mirror crash
segments.summary: Roller skates date to the 1700s: Dutch wooden spool skates, a 1743 London stage production using roller skates, and John Joseph Merlin's 1760 skates that led to him crashing into a mirror while playing violin at a masquerade ball.

segments.title: Plimpton's quad rocking skates and roller rink boom
segments.summary: James Leonard Plimpton, a New York furniture store owner, invented the 1863 rocking skates, the first quad skates with trucks; he demonstrated and promoted roller skating, and by the 1880s there were about 3,000 rinks worldwide.

segments.title: Victorian rinks, Charlie Chaplin, and the 1950s peak
segments.summary: Victorian rinks used organ music; the Grand Hall Olympia rink was built in London; skating moved into vaudeville and film, with Charlie Chaplin skating blindfolded and Professor Frank's daughter Lily skating on stilts. Rinks had a seedy reputation until operators rebranded them, and the 1950s saw more than 5,000 rinks.

segments.title: Roller skating and civil rights
segments.summary: Roller rinks were targets for sit-ins and integration; a 1963 sit-in occurred at White City roller rink in Chicago; Ledger Smith skated nearly 700 miles to the March on Washington; after 1964 rinks set aside Soul Nights or Martin Luther King Jr. Night for Black patrons.

segments.title: Soul music, disco, and roller disco
segments.summary: Soul Nights brought R&B, soul, and funk to rinks, changing skating culture. Bill Butler pushed rinks to play records and was central to disco spreading into roller skating at Empire Roller Disco in Brooklyn. Rinks converted to disco-style venues with neon, mirror balls, and sound systems. Polyurethane wheels in the 1970s allowed outdoor skating and smoother control; skateboard wheel makers moved into skates. 1970s films and TV, including Skatetown, U.S.A., Roller Boogie, Warriors, Chips, and Hell on Wheels by Sha Na Na and Flippers, are discussed.

segments.title: Skating styles: rhythm, jam, freestyle, regional
segments.summary: Discussion of rhythm skating, jam skating (breakdance on skates, b-boy battles), artistic skating, freestyle dance skating, regional styles in Atlanta, Cleveland, Detroit (sliding), and Chicago, plus the snoopy move and couple skating.

segments.title: Inline skates and skate anatomy
segments.summary: Inline skates arrived around 1983 and became popular in the 1990s; aggressive skating; Amish teenagers adopting rollerblades. Skate parts include boots (high-top vs low-top), plates, trucks, wheels (size and hardness, light-up wheels), toe stops (1876), and jam plugs.
topics: high top vs low top skates

segments.title: Pandemic skating revival and N.W.A trivia
segments.summary: Roller skating became popular during the pandemic, with actress Onalee Koto's TikTok videos sparking a Gen Z revival; Miranda Hawkins also took up skating. Trivia: N.W.A's first concert was at Skateland in Compton.

segments.title: Listener mail: John Green and Paper Towns correction
segments.summary: A listener corrects the hosts: the Paper Towns author is John Green, not Tom Green, who is a different comedian and co-founder of VidCon. John Green also co-hosts Dear Hank and John and hosts The Anthropocene Reviewed.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and give the email address for listener mail.
